title: Single or double quotes
idea: Python lets you use single ' ' or double " " quotes. Both work the same — but they must match.

exercises.prompt: print('Hi') and print("Hi") both show the same thing.
exercises.explanation: Single and double quotes work the same way. Both show: Hi

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a valid piece of text?
exercises.explanation: The quotes must MATCH: open and close with the same kind. 'cat' is fine; mixing ' and " is not.

exercises.prompt:
What is wrong with this?

print("Hello')
options: The quotes don't match (starts with ", ends with ')
exercises.explanation: It opens with " but closes with '. Quotes must be the same kind on both ends.

exercises.prompt: Build an instruction using SINGLE quotes to show: hello
exercises.explanation: Single quotes work just like double quotes: print('hello') shows hello.

exercises.prompt: You must always use double quotes in Python.
exercises.explanation: Single quotes are just as valid. Pick one style and keep both ends matching.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are valid? (pick all)
exercises.explanation: The first two have matching quotes. The third mixes quote types; the fourth has no quotes at all.

exercises.prompt:
Fix this so the quotes match:

print('Bye____)
exercises.explanation: It opened with a single quote, so it must close with a single quote: print('Bye').
Single quotes mark the text and aren't shown. Output: Dailo.

exercises.prompt: Which one will cause a problem?
exercises.explanation: The first opens with " and closes with ' — mismatched. The rest all match correctly.

exercises.prompt: Build an instruction using DOUBLE quotes to show: good job
exercises.explanation: print("good job") — matching double quotes around the whole phrase.
